strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: the limited generalization and scalability of tool-based SWE agents, and proposes an expressive IDE-based computer-use paradigm as an alternative.

The PwP environment is a substantial engineering contribution, integrating a modified VSCode IDE, Docker sandboxing, screen/video capture, xdotool actions, checkpointing, and a gymnasium-style API for multimodal, language-agnostic SWE tasks.

PwP-Bench unifies a broad set of 15 SWE tasks and 5400 instances across multiple languages, modalities, and task categories, with a Lite split intended to make evaluation tractable; this could be a useful testbed for future agents.

The empirical study is broad, evaluating five vision-language models under two agent configurations, and includes useful qualitative analyses of visual grounding failures, tool-use failures, and error recovery.

The assisted-tool experiments provide useful evidence that IDE tools and API-like operations can substantially improve performance, highlighting a concrete direction for future training and agent design.
The paper is generally well written, with clear motivation, good positioning relative to prior work, and informative comparison tables.
weaknesses: The central claim that computer-use agents can approach or surpass specialized tool-based SWE agents is not fully supported. Pure pixel-based keyboard/mouse agents perform very poorly (about 10% overall), and the strong results rely on file/bash API operations, which are themselves hand-engineered tools; per-task results also lag prior state of the art on many datasets.

The evaluation is limited to PwP-Bench-Lite (300 out of 5400 instances) and a 20-step cap, creating high variance and making it unclear how results generalize to the full benchmark or longer-horizon tasks. Confidence intervals and statistical tests are largely absent.

Comparisons with prior state-of-the-art methods are not apples-to-apples: different model versions, budgets, tooling, and evaluation conditions are used, and the aggregate average across heterogeneous metrics may obscure large per-task failures.

The benchmark is mostly an aggregation of 13 existing datasets plus only two new task suites, so the novelty of the tasks themselves is limited; aggregating heterogeneous metrics into an 'Overall Avg' is also methodologically questionable.

Reproducibility details are insufficient in the manuscript: the set-of-marks implementation, VSCode modifications, prompting/action formatting, task setup, and exact evaluation protocols are not fully specified, and no code/benchmark release link is evident.

The experiments lack training or fine-tuning of computer-use agents, open-weight or alternative computer-use baselines, and controlled ablations isolating the effect of the environment versus tool APIs. The assisted experiments manually engineer tool APIs per dataset, making it unclear how much is learned versus provided.
Ethical and safety considerations for agents with file/bash/OS access are only minimally addressed as sandboxing; broader dual-use, security, and failure-mode implications are not discussed in depth.

strengths: The paper explores a timely and interesting direction: using computer-use agents that interact with an IDE through screenshots, typing, and clicking for software engineering tasks.
The engineering effort behind PwP is nontrivial: a VSCode-based Dockerized environment, checkpointing, gymnasium-style API, parallelized evaluation, and support for multiple modalities and languages.
PwP-Bench aggregates a broad set of existing SWE and code-generation benchmarks into a unified interface, with execution-based evaluation and both code and non-code SWE tasks.
The qualitative analysis highlights important failure modes of current VLM agents, including poor visual grounding, file-editing errors, ineffective tool use, and inability to recover from mistakes.
The paper provides useful negative results showing that purely primitive computer-use agents struggle severely, while API/tool-assisted agents perform much better.
weaknesses: The central claim that computer-use agents can approach or surpass specialized tool-based agents is not adequately supported. The comparison to 'previous state of the art' uses reported numbers from different models, different system designs, different budgets, and often much longer trajectories, not a controlled evaluation of tool-based baselines inside PwP.

The paper does not actually evaluate strong tool-based SWE agents (e.g., SWE-Agent, OpenHands, Agentless) under the same PwP environment and same 20-step budget, despite claiming existing agents can be incorporated. This makes the core paradigm comparison unconvincing.

There is an internal contradiction: the best-performing 'computer-use' setting uses file and bash API operations, and the 'assisted' analysis uses hand-engineered per-task tools. These are precisely the predefined tool APIs the paper argues against, yet they drive most of the performance gains.

The pure visual computer-use setting also relies on Set-of-Marks annotations, i.e., interface-element parses, so it is not purely visual perception. This weakens the claimed advantage over accessibility/tool-based interfaces.

Evaluation is severely limited: experiments use only PwP-Bench-Lite (300 instances), a maximum of 20 iterations, five VLMs, and no multiple seeds or confidence intervals for most results. Long-horizon SWE tasks are especially affected by the 20-step cap.

The benchmark mostly repackages 13 existing datasets rather than introducing many genuinely new SWE tasks. The two new task sets are potentially interesting, but their size, difficulty, and validation are not sufficiently described.

Averaging heterogeneous metrics across 15 datasets into a single 'Overall Avg' is questionable. The previous-SOTA row is not a single system's score, so matching or exceeding that average does not imply a fair comparison.

The analysis of failure modes is largely qualitative and anecdotal. The paper would be stronger with quantified error rates for grounding failures, tool-use failures, repeated-action failures, and recovery behavior.

Reproducibility and artifact availability are unclear. The environment requires substantial modifications to VSCode, yet there is no clear statement that the code, benchmark, prompts, and evaluation scripts will be released, making independent validation difficult.

The paper overstates novelty and positioning. 'First software engineering-focused computer-use environment' is a strong claim that is not carefully substantiated against prior IDE, OS, and web-agent environments, and the contribution is largely integration plus evaluation rather than a new method.
Ethical and security implications of computer-use agents operating IDEs are not discussed, despite obvious risks around automated code execution, credential access, and misuse.

strengths: Introduces PwP, a unified IDE-based computer-use environment for SWE agents, with expressive primitive action space and access to all IDE tools across languages and modalities without per-task tool engineering.
PwP-Bench aggregates 15 diverse SWE tasks and 5400 instances across 8 languages and multiple modalities, including new IDE configuration and general SWE tasks, offering potential as a common testbed.

Provides a first systematic evaluation of general-purpose computer-use agents on SWE tasks, testing multiple VLMs and two action-space configurations, with useful analyses of visual grounding, IDE tool use, and assisted tooling.
Infrastructure contributions are substantial: sandboxed Docker/VSCode environment, state checkpointing, gym-like API, parallel evaluation, and support for future RL/search-based methods.
weaknesses: The main evaluation uses only PwP-Bench-Lite (300 instances; 20 samples per dataset) and caps agents at 20 steps, making results noisy and likely unrepresentative of full benchmark performance, especially for long-horizon SWE tasks.

Comparisons to prior state-of-the-art are not apples-to-apples: reported SOTA numbers use different models, budgets, prompts, and domain-specific tools, so the claim that computer-use agents 'approach or even surpass' specialized agents is not convincingly supported, especially given primitive-only agents average 10.2%.

The benchmark largely aggregates existing datasets; the newly introduced IDE-configuration and General-SWE tasks are small and insufficiently described/evaluated, and macro-averaging heterogeneous metrics may obscure per-task performance.

The assisted experiments cover only four datasets with manually engineered tools; they show potential but do not fully validate the central claim that better IDE tool use or agent training would broadly improve SWE performance.

Reproducibility is unclear: there is no explicit statement of code/data release, agent prompts, full implementation details, task adaptation procedures, or evaluation scripts for the complex environment.

Some claims are overstated: the strongest configuration uses file/bash API operations and assisted tools, so the framing of operating 'without hand-engineered tools' is misleading, while true primitive computer-use performance remains low.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely question: whether generalist computer-use agents can perform software engineering through visual IDE interaction, which is under-explored relative to web/OS benchmarks.

Introduces PwP, a VSCode-based sandboxed environment with expressive keyboard/mouse actions, execution-based rewards, checkpointing, Docker isolation, and a Gymnasium-style interface, making it a potentially useful platform for evaluating CUAs.
PwP-Bench is broad in scope: 15 task types / 5400 instances across multiple languages and modalities, unifying 13 existing benchmarks and adding two new IDE-specific and general-SWE task sets.
Execution-based verification is a strength: tasks are evaluated programmatically (unit tests, compilation, IDE state, metrics), reducing reliance on subjective or human judgment.
The evaluation covers nine CUA models across multiple configurations and includes qualitative and quantitative failure analysis, especially around visual grounding and use of IDE tools.
The assisted-agent experiment provides useful evidence that better tool/IDE utilization could substantially improve performance, highlighting headroom for future agents.
The paper is generally well-motivated and clearly positions SWE as a challenging domain for evaluating generalist computer-use agents.
The release of an environment and benchmark, if fully open-sourced and maintained, could be a valuable community resource.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the environment mainly integrates existing tools (VSCode, xdotool, Docker, VNC/ffmpeg), and the benchmark mostly ports 13 existing datasets rather than introducing fundamentally new SWE tasks; only two new task families are proposed, each with 20 instances.

The main evaluation is on PwP-Bench-Lite (300 instances, 20 per task) rather than the full 5400-instance benchmark, with no confidence intervals, variance estimates, or multiple seeds, so many reported differences may be statistically fragile.

The 20-step cap in the main experiments is too short for many SWE tasks; long-horizon evaluation is limited to only one model on three SWE-Bench datasets, so the primary conclusions may not hold under realistic budgets.

The specialized-agent baseline in the main table is only mini-sweagent; comparisons to best reported specialized SWE agents are informal, use different subsets/metrics, and are not apples-to-apples, weakening claims that CUAs 'reach' specialist performance.

The headline result that adding file-editing and bash APIs brings CUAs near specialized agents is somewhat expected and changes the setting substantially; it does not demonstrate that purely visual computer use is competitive.

Task selection and benchmark construction are not sufficiently validated: there is little evidence that ported tasks preserve difficulty under visual IDE interaction, no human/expert calibration for the new tasks, and no analysis of contamination or saturation.

The visual-grounding failure analysis is based on manually inspecting only 20 trajectories per model and uses somewhat subjective error definitions; reported error rates are also inconsistently described.

Reproducibility is only partially demonstrated: the manuscript promises open-source release, but no explicit code/data link is visible in the text, and full evaluation depends on costly proprietary models and large-scale Docker execution.
Several claims are stronger than the evidence, e.g., 'often reaching the levels of specialized agents' despite large category-level gaps and limited baselines.

strengths: Introduces a VSCode-based computer-use environment and PwP-Bench for software engineering, with execution-based rewards and support for multiple languages and modalities.
Provides a broad evaluation across multiple closed- and open-weight models under two computer-use agent setups, plus a specialized SWE baseline.
Includes useful qualitative and quantitative analyses of failure modes such as visual grounding errors, poor file editing, and limited use of advanced IDE tooling.
The gymnasium-style interface, sandboxed Docker setup, and checkpointing support could be valuable for future benchmarking and agent development if fully released.
weaknesses: Main evaluation is on PwP-Bench-Lite, with only 20 instances per task, which is far too small for stable conclusions; most comparisons lack confidence intervals, variance estimates, or statistical tests.

The central claim that computer-use agents can approach specialized SWE agents is supported mainly by a hybrid setup using file and bash APIs. These APIs bypass visual interaction and are essentially the core tools of specialized agents, so the comparison does not demonstrate pixel-based SWE ability.

Benchmark novelty is limited: 13 of 15 tasks are ported from existing datasets, and the newly introduced VSCode and General-SWE tasks contain only around 40 instances total. This weakens the claim of a 'first comprehensive' benchmark.

Only one specialized baseline, mini-sweagent with Claude-4.0, is run on the same instances. Reported best specialized scores for other datasets are not evaluated on the same small subsets, making the specialized comparison weak and potentially misleading.

The visual grounding analysis is internally inconsistent: Section 5.1 reports 20% for GPT-4o and 95% for Claude-Sonnet-4.0, while Appendix F swaps these numbers (95% for GPT-4o, 20% for Claude-Sonnet-4.0). This undermines a key failure-mode analysis.

The CUA+File/Bash design changes the observation protocol (screenshots only when requested) and adds powerful text APIs, so performance gains cannot be cleanly attributed to improved computer-use capability; ablations isolating these factors are missing.

Several benchmark tasks can be solved entirely through text/bash/file APIs, so the benchmark does not consistently test visual IDE control. The best results often reflect API use rather than 'programming with pixels.'

Reproducibility is insufficient: there is no visible code/repository link, and the paper lacks full prompts, action formats, Set-of-Marks details, and other implementation specifics needed to replicate the modified VSCode environment.
The POMDP formalization is superficial and does not meaningfully inform the experimental design or analysis.

Writing and presentation contain typos and inconsistencies (e.g., 'Aas,' 'Sweench,' 'GUS-Owl,' 'DoM,' 'offcail'), and some claims are stronger than the evidence, such as describing General-SWE performance as minimal when non-trivial scores are reported.

strengths: Introduces PwP, a timely and useful computer-use environment for software engineering with a VSCode-based IDE, primitive keyboard/mouse actions, Docker isolation, execution-based rewards, and checkpointing.
Provides PwP-Bench, a large unified benchmark of 15 SWE task families and 5400 instances spanning multiple languages and modalities, including two new IDE-specific/general SWE task sets.

Conducts an extensive empirical study across nine models and three agent designs (pure CUA, CUA+file/bash APIs, and specialized mini-sweagent), with additional long-horizon results for SWE-Bench tasks.
Offers insightful qualitative and quantitative failure analysis, especially on visual grounding, poor use of advanced IDE tools, limited error recovery, and reliance on memorized action sequences.
The assisted-tool experiments usefully quantify performance headroom and support the claim that better tool-use training could substantially improve CUAs.
The environment and benchmark are designed for reproducibility and extensibility, with a gymnasium interface, configuration-based task setup, and plans for open-source release.
weaknesses: The central comparison against specialized agents relies almost entirely on mini-sweagent; best reported SOTA SWE agents are much stronger, so the claim that CUAs can reach "specialist-level" performance is not fully supported by the main experiments.

The benchmark is largely a unification of 13 existing datasets, and the two newly created task sets (VSCode and General-SWE) contain only 20 instances each, making those analyses relatively small and potentially anecdotal.
Most evaluations use PwP-Bench-Lite with a 20-step cap, which may unfairly penalize CUAs on long-horizon SWE tasks; the 250-step evaluation is limited to a few models and datasets.

There is a direct inconsistency in the visual grounding statistics: the main text reports 20% for GPT-4o and 95% for Claude-Sonnet-4.0, while the appendix reports 20% for Claude-Sonnet-4.0 and 95% for GPT-4o. This undermines a key claim and must be corrected.

The "pure" computer-use setting uses Set-of-Marks/DOM annotations, which is not strictly screenshot-only pixel interaction; the paper should more clearly separate this auxiliary-information setting from genuinely visual CUAs.
The aggregate scores average heterogeneous metrics across datasets, which can obscure task-specific performance and make cross-benchmark comparisons less interpretable.
Visual grounding error analysis is based on manual review of only 20 trajectories, with no inter-annotator agreement, and statistical significance is tested for only one result.
Some claims about tool use and error recovery are supported mainly by qualitative examples, and the paper does not include human baselines or detailed per-tool usage statistics.
